questions.stem: A latency-sensitive API backed by Lambda has slow responses after idle periods because of cold starts. What should the developer configure?

options.text: Reserved concurrency set to the expected peak request rate
options.rationale: Reserved concurrency limits and guarantees capacity but does not pre-initialize it.

options.text: A longer timeout
options.rationale: Timeout does not affect start-up time.

options.text: A dead-letter queue
options.rationale: DLQs hold failed asynchronous events.

options.text: Provisioned concurrency on the function's alias
options.rationale: Pre-initialized execution environments respond without cold-start delay.

questions.explanation: Slow responses after idle periods point to cold starts, which provisioned concurrency removes by keeping environments initialized. Reserved concurrency is the nearest distractor, but it limits and guarantees capacity without pre-initializing it.

questions.stem: Many concurrent Lambda functions open their own connections to an Amazon RDS database and exhaust its connection limit. What should the developer add?

options.text: Amazon RDS Proxy between the functions and the database
options.rationale: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections.

options.text: A larger Lambda memory setting
options.rationale: More memory does not reduce connections.

options.text: An Amazon SQS queue between the functions and the database
options.rationale: A queue does not pool connections; whatever consumes it still connects to the database.

options.text: A CloudFront distribution in front of the database
options.rationale: CloudFront caches HTTP content, not database connections.

questions.explanation: Connection pooling protects databases from bursts of short-lived clients.

questions.stem: A Lambda function creates a new SDK client and database connection inside its handler on every invocation. How can the developer reduce latency for warm invocations?

options.text: Close the connection at the end of every invocation
options.rationale: Closing it forces a new connection on the next invocation, which is the slow part.

options.text: Create the client and connection outside the handler
options.rationale: Code outside the handler runs once per execution environment, and later invocations reuse it.

options.text: Increase the function's timeout so the connection has time to open
options.rationale: Timeout does not make invocations faster.

options.text: Move the client code into an environment variable
options.rationale: Environment variables hold settings, not objects.

questions.explanation: Initialize expensive resources once per environment, outside the handler.

questions.stem: A Lambda function mostly waits on an external API. Its reports show that it uses a small fraction of its configured memory, and its duration does not change when memory is increased. How can the developer lower cost?

options.text: Increase the memory setting so that each invocation finishes faster
options.rationale: Duration does not drop for I/O-bound work, so cost rises.

options.text: Add provisioned concurrency
options.rationale: Provisioned concurrency adds cost to reduce cold starts.

options.text: Lower the memory setting and check that duration stays the same
options.rationale: Lambda charges by memory and duration, so lower memory with the same duration costs less.

options.text: Move the function into a VPC
options.rationale: VPC access does not reduce compute cost.

questions.explanation: Right-size memory from measured usage and duration; CPU-bound and I/O-bound functions behave differently.

questions.stem: Several services subscribe to one Amazon SNS topic, but each needs only some message types. Each subscriber currently receives every message and discards most of them in code. What should the developer do?

options.text: Replace the topic with one Amazon SQS queue that all services poll
options.rationale: Each queue message is processed by one consumer, so the services would split the messages instead of each getting the ones it needs.

options.text: Increase the subscribers' Lambda memory
options.rationale: Faster discarding still processes unwanted messages.

options.text: Turn on SNS message archiving
options.rationale: Archiving keeps messages for replay; it does not filter deliveries.

options.text: Add a filter policy to each subscription
options.rationale: SNS delivers only the messages that match each subscription's filter.

questions.explanation: The clue is subscribers discarding most messages in code: a filter policy makes SNS deliver only matching messages to each subscription. One shared queue is the trap, because each queue message goes to only one consumer.

questions.stem: Consumers poll an Amazon SQS queue constantly, and most receive calls return no messages, which increases cost. Which changes will reduce the number of API calls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Send, receive and delete messages in batches
options.rationale: Batch actions handle up to ten messages per request, so fewer calls are needed.

options.text: Switch to a FIFO queue
options.rationale: FIFO adds ordering and exactly-once processing, not fewer empty receives.

options.text: Turn on long polling by setting a receive wait time
options.rationale: Long polling waits for messages to arrive instead of returning empty responses.

options.text: Poll more often with short polling so messages are picked up sooner
options.rationale: More frequent short polls make more empty calls.

options.text: Increase the visibility timeout
options.rationale: Visibility timeout affects redelivery, not empty receives.

questions.explanation: Long polling and batching are the main ways to reduce SQS request costs.

questions.stem: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway returns the same product catalog for several minutes at a time, and the backend is under heavy load from repeated GET requests. What should the developer do?

options.text: Enable API caching on the stage with a suitable TTL
options.rationale: API Gateway serves cached responses and calls the backend less often.

options.text: Increase the stage's throttling limits for GET requests
options.rationale: Higher limits let even more requests reach the backend.

options.text: Switch to a Lambda proxy integration
options.rationale: The integration type does not reduce repeated calls.

options.text: Add a request validator
options.rationale: Validation rejects bad requests; it does not cache good ones.

questions.explanation: The clue is repeated GET requests for a response that stays the same for minutes, so cache it on the stage. Raising throttling limits is the trap: it lets even more requests reach the busy backend.

questions.stem: Static images in a private Amazon S3 bucket load slowly for users far from the bucket's Region. The bucket must stay private. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Allow the CloudFront distribution to read objects in the bucket policy
options.rationale: With OAC, the bucket policy grants the CloudFront service principal read access, limited to that distribution, so the bucket stays private.

options.text: Turn on S3 Versioning for the bucket
options.rationale: Versioning keeps object versions; it does not speed delivery.

options.text: Make the bucket public and give users the direct S3 URL for each image file
options.rationale: This removes privacy and does not cache content near users.

options.text: Serve the images through a CloudFront distribution that uses OAC
options.rationale: CloudFront caches the images at edge locations, and origin access control signs its requests to the bucket.

options.text: Move the images to the S3 Standard-IA storage class
options.rationale: Storage classes change cost and retrieval terms, not distance to users.

questions.explanation: CloudFront caches content near users, and OAC plus a bucket policy for the distribution keeps the origin private. Making the bucket public is the trap: it opens the data and still does not cache anything near users.

questions.stem: An application runs as several Amazon ECS services. The developer needs to find which service is running out of CPU and memory. Which feature should the developer use?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail
options.rationale: CloudTrail records API calls, not resource usage.

options.text: Amazon ECR image scanning
options.rationale: Scanning checks images for vulnerabilities.

options.text: CloudWatch Container Insights
options.rationale: Container Insights collects CPU, memory and other metrics for clusters, services and tasks.

options.text: AWS CodeDeploy deployment logs
options.rationale: Deployment logs describe deployments, not runtime usage.

questions.explanation: Container Insights shows resource bottlenecks for containerized workloads.

questions.stem: A web application on an EC2 Auto Scaling group is slow during busy hours and over-provisioned at night. The developer wants the group to keep average CPU near 50 percent automatically. Which scaling policy fits?

options.text: A scheduled action that adds instances during business hours
options.rationale: Schedules do not react to unexpected load.

options.text: A fixed desired capacity set to the daily peak
options.rationale: This wastes capacity at night.

options.text: Manual scaling by an operator
options.rationale: Manual changes are slow and error-prone.

options.text: A target tracking scaling policy on average CPU utilization
options.rationale: Target tracking adds and removes instances to hold the metric near the target.

questions.explanation: The clue is keeping average CPU near a target automatically, which is what target tracking does. A scheduled action is the nearest distractor, but it changes capacity at set times and does not react to actual load.

questions.stem: A Java Lambda function has slow cold starts because its framework takes several seconds to initialize. Traffic is unpredictable, and the team does not want to pay for idle pre-initialized environments. What should the developer turn on?

options.text: Provisioned concurrency on the function's alias
options.rationale: Provisioned concurrency keeps environments ready and is billed while they wait, which the team wants to avoid.

options.text: A larger ephemeral storage setting for /tmp
options.rationale: /tmp size does not affect framework initialization time.

options.text: Reserved concurrency set to the expected peak
options.rationale: Reserved concurrency caps and guarantees concurrency; it does not pre-initialize environments.

options.text: Lambda SnapStart on the function
options.rationale: SnapStart restores new environments from a cached snapshot of initialized state, which shortens cold starts.

questions.explanation: SnapStart cuts cold-start initialization time. For Java runtimes it has no additional cost, and there are no idle pre-initialized environments to pay for.

questions.stem: A Lambda function processes an Amazon SQS queue one message per invocation. Message volume is high, and the per-invocation overhead makes processing slow and costly. A short delay before processing is acceptable. What should the developer change on the event source mapping?

options.text: Raise the batch size and set a batching window
options.rationale: Larger batches, gathered over a short window, process more messages per invocation.

options.text: Lower the queue's visibility timeout
options.rationale: This controls when unprocessed messages reappear, not how many each invocation handles.

options.text: Set the maximum concurrency to 2
options.rationale: Limiting concurrency slows processing further.

options.text: Turn on long polling with a 20-second wait time
options.rationale: Lambda's event source mapping already polls the queue; this does not batch invocations.

questions.explanation: Batch size and the batching window trade a little latency for far fewer invocations.

questions.stem: A Node.js service on EC2 makes thousands of DynamoDB calls a minute through the AWS SDK. Profiling shows that a lot of time goes to setting up new TLS connections. What should the developer do?

options.text: Create a new SDK client for every request
options.rationale: That is the cause: each new client sets up new connections.

options.text: Reuse one SDK client with HTTP keep-alive
options.rationale: Reusing a client and its connection pool avoids a new TLS handshake for each call.

options.text: Switch every DynamoDB call to strongly consistent reads
options.rationale: Consistency does not affect connection setup.

options.text: Add a sleep between calls so connections can close cleanly
options.rationale: Waiting adds latency and does not reuse connections.

questions.explanation: Reuse SDK clients and keep connections alive to avoid repeated connection setup.

questions.stem: A new application's DynamoDB table gets unpredictable traffic: near zero most of the day, with sudden spikes. Requests are throttled during spikes, and capacity sits unused the rest of the time. What should the developer change?

options.text: Provision write capacity for the highest spike around the clock
options.rationale: This avoids throttling but pays for unused capacity most of the day.

options.text: Add a global secondary index to spread the traffic
options.rationale: Indexes serve other access patterns; they do not add capacity to the table.

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode
options.rationale: On-demand mode serves traffic as it arrives and bills per request, with no capacity to plan.

options.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams for the table
options.rationale: Streams record changes; they do not affect capacity.

questions.explanation: On-demand capacity suits unpredictable or spiky workloads.

questions.stem: A team wants better price-performance for its Python Lambda functions. The functions use only pure-Python libraries. What change should the developer consider first?

options.text: Raise every function's memory to the maximum
options.rationale: More memory raises cost and helps only CPU- or memory-bound functions.

options.text: Move every function into a VPC
options.rationale: VPC placement is for private resource access, not price-performance.

options.text: Turn on provisioned concurrency for every function
options.rationale: Provisioned concurrency adds cost to reduce cold starts; it does not improve price-performance.

options.text: Switch the functions' architecture to arm64 (AWS Graviton)
options.rationale: arm64 functions typically offer better price-performance, and pure-Python code runs without changes.

questions.explanation: Graviton (arm64) is a common, low-effort price-performance improvement for Lambda.

questions.stem: An application uploads 5 GB video files to Amazon S3 with a single PUT request. Uploads are slow, and a network error near the end means starting over. What should the developer do?

options.text: Use multipart upload, sending parts in parallel and retrying failed parts
options.rationale: Parts upload in parallel, and only a failed part is retried, not the whole file.

options.text: Compress each video into a ZIP archive before uploading
options.rationale: Video is already compressed, and the upload would still be one large request.

options.text: Turn on S3 Versioning on the bucket
options.rationale: Versioning keeps object versions; it does not speed up or resume uploads.

options.text: Upload each file to an Amazon EBS volume first
options.rationale: This adds a step and does not fix how the file reaches S3.

questions.explanation: Multipart upload improves throughput and resilience for large objects.

questions.stem: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway has high p99 latency. The developer must find out whether the time is spent in API Gateway itself or in the backend integration. Which CloudWatch metrics should the developer compare?

options.text: 4XXError and 5XXError
options.rationale: Error counts show failures, not where time is spent.

options.text: Latency and IntegrationLatency
options.rationale: IntegrationLatency is the backend's time; Latency is the full request, so the gap is API Gateway's own overhead.

options.text: Count and CacheHitCount
options.rationale: These show request volume and cache use, not timing.

options.text: The Lambda function's Invocations and Throttles
options.rationale: These show how often the function ran and was throttled, not latency.

questions.explanation: Comparing Latency with IntegrationLatency separates API Gateway overhead from backend time.

questions.stem: A team runs an AWS Step Functions workflow millions of times a day to process events. Each run lasts a few seconds and can safely be repeated. Workflow costs are high. What should the developer change?

options.text: Add more Wait states so that runs spread out over time
options.rationale: Waiting does not change the per-run cost model.

options.text: Split each workflow into two Standard workflows
options.rationale: This doubles the number of Standard executions.

options.text: Use an Express workflow instead of a Standard workflow
options.rationale: Express workflows are designed for high-volume, short-duration workloads and are priced for them.

options.text: Run the workflow from an EC2 instance instead of from Lambda
options.rationale: Where the start call comes from does not change workflow costs.

questions.explanation: Choose Express workflows for high-volume, short, idempotent work; Standard for long-running, exactly-once workflows.

questions.stem: A CloudFront distribution in front of an API serves product pages that rarely change, but its cache hit ratio is low and most requests reach the origin. Which changes will raise the cache hit ratio? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use a CachingDisabled cache policy for the product pages
options.rationale: Disabling caching sends every request to the origin.

options.text: Remove unneeded headers, cookies and query strings from the cache key
options.rationale: Every value in the cache key splits the cache; keeping only what changes the response raises the hit ratio.

options.text: Add the User-Agent header to the cache key
options.rationale: User-Agent varies widely, so it splits the cache further.

options.text: Turn on origin access control for the API origin
options.rationale: Origin access control restricts direct access to supported AWS origins; it does not change the cache key or TTLs.

options.text: Have the origin send Cache-Control max-age values that suit the content
options.rationale: Longer, appropriate TTLs keep objects in the cache longer.

questions.explanation: A smaller cache key and suitable TTLs raise the CloudFront cache hit ratio.
